title: One-Way Doors
explain: A one-way door is a decision you cannot easily walk back through, because the cost of reversing it is other people and stored data depending on it, not your own engineering effort. In system design the three that matter are the API, the data flow and the data model. I hold those to a very high standard and decide everything else fast.
model:
The three classic one-way doors:

- **API:** once clients integrate, every field name, meaning, error code and default is a contract. Removing or re-interpreting one breaks someone you cannot redeploy.
- **Data flow:** who produces which event, who consumes it, what the message means. Downstream consumers build on it.
- **Data model:** how data is shaped, keyed and stored. Migrating billions of rows, or changing the meaning of an ID already in URLs and other tables, is slow and risky.

How to treat them: review with consumers, write them down, think about what you will want in two years, and prefer designs that **grow additively** (new optional fields, endpoints, event types).

```
breaking change, safely:
add new field/version beside the old -> announce deprecation, help migrate
   -> watch old traffic fall to ~0 -> remove old
```

Everything else is a [two-way door](#/sd/f/two-way-door). The skill is *sorting* decisions into the right bucket and spending scarce care on the first. Compare how [high-level thinking](#/sd/f/high-level-thinking) flags what to scrutinise.

details.q: Which of these is a one-way door: a public response field, a table other services read, an internal cache eviction policy, an event three teams consume, a replica count?
details.a: The response field, the shared table and the event. They have external dependents. Eviction policy and replica count are internal knobs changeable with a deploy and nobody else notices.

details.q: A public API returned `"price": 12.5` in dollars and you now want integer cents. Why is that painful?
details.a: Clients parse the published field, so silently changing type or unit breaks everyone you cannot redeploy. The remedy is additive evolution: add `price_cents`, deprecate the old field, migrate callers. Modelling money as integer minor units up front would have avoided it.

details.q: How do you make a breaking change to a published API without breaking clients?
details.a: Run both versions side by side, announce deprecation and help clients migrate, monitor traffic on the old version until it reaches roughly zero, then remove it. Removing first and fixing complaints later is how outages are made.

details.q: A teammate wants a three-week review on whether a new internal service is one process or two. Response?
details.a: Decide fast; process layout is a two-way door if code boundaries are clean. Spend the review time on the API other teams will call.

details.q: Why is data modelling a one-way door even when you own the database?
details.a: Because stored data and IDs leak into other tables, URLs, caches, exports and downstream consumers. Changing keys or meanings means migrating all of them, usually online and with dual writes.

details.q: What habit lowers the risk of a one-way door?
details.a: Design for additive growth, review with the consumers before shipping, write the contract down, and version any unavoidable break.

prompts.q: Explain one-way doors and name the three that matter in system design.
points: Hard to reverse because others and stored data depend on it
Cost is outside your own code
Hold them to a very high standard

prompts.q: You must change a published API field's meaning. Walk through how you roll it out.
points: Add new field or version beside the old one
Remove only when usage is near zero

prompts.q: Sort these into one-way and two-way doors and justify: cache TTL, event schema, instance type, URL ID format, internal module layout.
points: Event schema and URL ID format are one-way
TTL, instance type and module layout are two-way
Reason is external dependents versus a local deploy
Spend review effort proportional to irreversibility
